title: The Snowman Is Mostly Air
blurb: Why snow packs, where snowmen came from, and how one in Maine grew to 122 feet tall.

blocks.text: Snow is soft and cold and white. Roll a little ball of snow on the ground. It gets bigger and bigger. Roll a big ball. Then roll a middle ball. Then roll a small one for the head. 2.title: The Snowman Is Mostly Air
2.subtitle: A reading sheet for ages 5 to 6

blocks.prompt: The Right Kind of Snow
blocks.text: A snowman needs the right kind of snow. When the day is very cold, the snow is dry and powdery. It slips apart in your hands and will not hold together. When the snow is close to melting, it is a little bit wet. That wet skin lets the tiny crystals grab each other and hold on. That is packing snow. Roll a snowball across the yard and it picks up more snow with every turn. It grows fast. Stack three balls with the biggest one at the bottom, and your snowman can stand up. Here is the strange part. Fresh snow is mostly air. Your snowman is not a solid block of ice. He is a fluffy pile of crystals with air in all the gaps.

the biggest one
air

answers: powdery

3.title: The Snowman Is Mostly Air
3.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: The oldest known drawing of one is from 1380
Michelangelo once sculpted snow

Snow is free and easy to shape
Every snowman melts in the end

blocks.prompt: The Statue That Always Melts
blocks.text:
People have been building snowmen for a very long time. The oldest picture of one that anyone has found sits in the corner of a book made in the year 1380. It is a prayer book from Europe, and in the margin somebody drew a snow figure sitting beside a fire. Nobody wrote down who built the first snowman, and nobody ever will. Snow arrives free, it is easy to shape, and children work out what to do with it without being taught.

In 1494 a young sculptor named Michelangelo was asked to make a statue out of snow for a powerful family in Florence, Italy. He would later carve some of the most famous marble statues in the world. That winter he carved snow instead, and his snow statue melted away like every other one.

In the winter of 1511 the city of Brussels was buried in snow, and the people filled the streets with more than a hundred snow figures. Some were funny, some were rude, and some told the city what its rulers were doing wrong. Crowds walked around for weeks to look at them. Then a warm week arrived and the whole show was gone.

A snowman is the only kind of statue that everybody knows will disappear. Maybe that is why we keep making them.

4.title: The Snowman Is Mostly Air
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Snow crystals always have six sides
Water vapor freezes straight onto dust
Shape depends on temperature and humidity
Ukichiro Nakaya grew snow in a lab in the 1930s
He called snow crystals letters sent from the sky

blocks.prompt: Every Snowman Starts as a Cloud
blocks.text:
Every snowman begins high in a cloud, long before anyone gets a shovel. Up there, water is floating around as vapor, an invisible gas. When the air gets cold enough, some of that vapor freezes directly onto a floating speck of dust without ever becoming a drop of water first. That first grain of ice is the seed of a snow crystal.

Water molecules can only stack one way when they freeze. Each molecule links to its neighbors at a fixed angle, and the pattern those angles build has six sides. That is why a snow crystal grows six arms, never five and never seven. The shape of the whole crystal is set by the shape of the molecule inside it.

What the crystal grows into depends on the trip it takes down. Just below freezing it tends to spread into flat six sided plates. A few degrees colder and it builds hollow columns and thin needles instead. Around five degrees Fahrenheit, in air loaded with moisture, it grows the wide feathery star that people draw on windows. A falling crystal drifts through layers of different temperature and different dampness, and each layer adds another stage to its shape. That is why the finished crystals look so different from one another.

A Japanese physicist named Ukichiro Nakaya worked all of this out in the 1930s. He grew snow crystals in a cold laboratory, one at a time, on the tip of a rabbit hair, changing the temperature and the moisture until he could produce any shape he wanted. He said a snow crystal is a letter sent from the sky. If you know how to read it, the crystal tells you what the air was doing while it fell.

5.title: The Snowman Is Mostly Air
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fresh snow can be over 90 percent air
Snow looks white because it scatters every color
Ice bonds where crystals touch, which is called sintering
Snow can vanish without melting, by sublimation
Animals shelter in the warm gap under the snowpack

blocks.prompt: Why Snow Is White, and Why It Sticks
blocks.text:
Ice is clear. Hold a cube up to the window and you can see straight through it. So why is a snowdrift blindingly white, when every crystal in it is made of the same clear ice?

The answer is surfaces. A single ice crystal lets light pass through, bending it a little on the way. A drift holds billions of crystals, each with faces pointing every direction, packed loosely with air between them. Light entering the pile bounces from face to face, scattering again and again until it is thrown back out. Ice scatters all the colors of light roughly equally, so what comes back out is the whole mix, and the whole mix looks white to us. Sea foam and crushed glass turn white for exactly the same reason. Break clear stuff into enough pieces and you get white.

All that space between the crystals matters in another way. Fresh snow can be more than ninety percent air by volume. That trapped air makes snow a good insulator, which is why a layer of snow keeps the ground beneath it warmer than the open sky above. Mice, voles, and shrews spend the whole winter in the gap between the soil and the snowpack, tunneling around in the dark while the air above is far colder.

Stickiness is a separate question. Snow packs best when it is near thirty two degrees Fahrenheit, because at that temperature the crystals carry a thin slippery film on their surfaces. Press two crystals together and that film refreezes across the join, welding them at every point where they touch. Scientists call this process sintering. A snowball is not squeezed, it is welded. That is also why a snowball made at ten degrees below zero falls apart in your glove. There is no film, so there is nothing to weld with.

Melting is not the only way a snowman leaves. On a dry, sunny, freezing day, ice can pass straight from solid to vapor without ever becoming water. That is called sublimation, and it is why a snowman can shrink for a week without a single drip landing on the ground.

6.title: The Snowman Is Mostly Air
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Snow crystals form by deposition, gas straight to solid
Sintering welds crystals where they touch
Snow is a loose foam of ice and trapped air
Olympia, Bethel, Maine, 2008: 122 feet 1 inch tall
Surface area to volume decides what melts first
The oldest known snowman drawing dates to 1380

blocks.prompt: The Cheapest Sculpture in the World
blocks.text:
A snowman is the most democratic sculpture ever invented. The material is free, it delivers itself to your door, no tool is required, and the finished work is guaranteed to be destroyed. Perhaps that is why the practice is so old. The earliest known drawing of one appears in the margin of a European prayer book from 1380, and by 1494 the sculptor Michelangelo was building one on commission for a wealthy family in Florence. Nobody invented the snowman. It is simply what people do when snow falls and they have an afternoon.

The physics underneath it is more interesting than the tradition. Snow does not begin as frozen rain. High in a cloud, water vapor freezes directly onto a floating speck of dust, skipping the liquid stage entirely, a change called deposition. Because water molecules bond at fixed angles, the growing crystal can only take a six sided form. Its finer detail is written by its journey: plates just below freezing, columns and needles a few degrees colder, elaborate feathered stars near five degrees Fahrenheit in moist air. The physicist Ukichiro Nakaya, who grew crystals one at a time in a cold laboratory in the 1930s, described a snow crystal as a letter sent from the sky. He meant it precisely. The shape is a record of the conditions the crystal passed through.

What lands on your lawn is not really a solid at all. Fresh snow is a loose foam of ice and trapped air, frequently more than ninety percent air by volume. That is why it insulates so well that mice tunnel comfortably beneath it all winter, and why it appears white despite being built from transparent ice. Billions of crystal faces scatter light in every direction and return every color at once, and every color at once is what our eyes read as white.

Building with the stuff depends on a narrow temperature window. Near thirty two degrees Fahrenheit, ice crystals carry an extremely thin film on their surfaces that behaves almost like liquid. Press two crystals together and that film refreezes across the contact point, bonding them permanently. The process is called sintering, and it means a snowball is welded rather than squeezed. Cold, dry powder has no such film, which is why the finest skiing snow makes the worst snowman.

Scale changes the problem. In 2008, the town of Bethel, Maine, built a snow figure named Olympia that stood 122 feet and 1 inch tall, with skis for eyelashes and whole spruce trees for arms. It required thousands of tons of snow and a great deal of heavy machinery, and although it was finished in February, it did not fully melt until July. That delay is not luck. Melting happens at the surface, and as any shape grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area. A giant snowman has a small skin for its enormous body, so it loses itself slowly. The same rule explains why your snowman always loses its head first.

And melting is not the only exit. In dry, sunny, freezing weather, ice can pass straight from solid to vapor without ever becoming water. Snowmen routinely shrink for days without a drip. The sculpture leaves the way it arrived, one molecule at a time, back into the air.
